title: Taxes
objective: After this level you can explain what taxes pay for and name the main kinds of tax.
summary: Taxes pay for what governments provide, about a third of GDP across rich countries. They fall on what you earn, buy and own; most countries use a VAT, the US does not.

cards.headline: In 1789, Benjamin Franklin named the only two sure things in life.
cards.body: One was death. The other was taxes. More than two centuries later, both are still going strong. So what do they actually pay for, and what exactly gets taxed?

cards.headline: What your taxes buy
cards.body: Taxes are how a government pays for the things it provides. In the US, the biggest federal items are national defense, Social Security, healthcare and interest on past borrowing. States and cities spend most on education, then on highways, libraries, parks, police and fire protection. So the fire truck racing down your street? You've already chipped in.

cards.fact: Across rich countries, taxes add up to about a third of the whole economy.
cards.context: In 2023, taxes averaged 33.9% of GDP (the value of everything a country produces in a year) across OECD countries. The range is wide: under a fifth in Mexico, over two-fifths in France and Denmark. How big that slice should be is a choice each country makes, and they choose very differently.

cards.headline: Three things to tax: what you earn, buy and own

items.label: What you earn
points: Income tax on wages and other income

items.label: What you buy
points: Excise taxes on gasoline, tobacco and alcohol

items.label: What you own
points: Property taxes, a mainstay for US states and cities
Estate taxes on what people leave behind

cards.fact: The US is the only OECD country without a VAT.
cards.context: A value-added tax is a sales tax collected in slices. Each business along the chain, from lumber yard to furniture maker, pays tax on its sales and gets credit for the tax already paid on its inputs. More than 170 countries use one. The US relies instead on state and local sales taxes, added at the till.

mascot.line: A VAT is a relay race: every runner carries the tax a little further, and the shopper crosses the finish line.

cards.headline: Taxes: sorted
learned: Taxes pay for what governments provide
Across the OECD, about a third of GDP
Taxed: what you earn, buy and own
A VAT is collected at every stage; the US has none

questions.prompt: Which of these is a tax on what you buy?

options.label: Estate tax
options.rationale: That taxes what people leave behind.

questions.explanation: A VAT, like a sales tax, falls on spending: it is a tax on what you buy.

questions.prompt: How is a VAT collected differently from a US-style sales tax?

options.label: Only people with high incomes pay it
options.rationale: Everyone who buys taxed goods pays it.

options.label: It is taken out of wages each payday
options.rationale: That's how income and payroll taxes work.

options.label: It is charged once a year on property
Each business in the chain pays on its sales, with credit for tax already paid

questions.explanation: A VAT is collected in slices at every stage of production; a US sales tax is added once, at the till.

questions.prompt: Part of today's US federal tax money pays for decisions made years ago. Which spending item is that?

options.label: Fire protection
options.rationale: That's a state and local service, and it's paid for today.

options.label: Parks and libraries
options.rationale: Those are mostly state and local spending.

options.label: Highways
options.rationale: Mostly state and local, and not a payment for past decisions.

questions.explanation: Interest on past borrowing is one of the biggest federal items: today's taxes paying for yesterday's borrowing. Level 54 follows that thread.
